title: Technical Product Management
summary: Product management for technical products — APIs, SDKs, developer tools and platforms. You own what the product does and why, for users who are developers.
tests: Whether you can find a developer's real problem, design an interface they will build on for years, write specs engineers trust, and measure adoption honestly.

distinct_from.how: A Technical Product Manager owns WHAT a technical product does and WHY: the developer problem, the API contract, adoption and success metrics. A Technical Program Manager owns HOW and WHEN a multi-team effort is delivered. Technical PM interviews look like product interviews with deeper technical content; they do not test critical paths or program governance.

rounds.title: Technical Product Sense
rounds.focus: Finding the developer's real problem and shaping the product around it.

rounds.title: API and Platform Design
rounds.focus: An interface other teams can build on: resources, errors, versioning, limits.

rounds.title: Specs and Engineering Partnership
rounds.focus: Writing requirements, not designs; deciding what to build at all.

rounds.title: Adoption and Developer Metrics
rounds.focus: Measuring a product whose users are developers, and moving them to a new version.

rounds.title: Behavioural
rounds.focus: Owning the what and the why while engineers own the how.

questions.title: Testing payments without real money
questions.prompt: You are the product manager for a payments API. Design a product that lets developers test their integration end to end without moving real money.
hints: What do developers need to test besides a successful payment?
How close to production must the test environment behave?
How do they move from test to live safely?
followups: Developers say tests pass but production fails. Why might that be?
How do you let developers simulate a bank outage?
How would you measure whether the sandbox is good?
criteria: Identifies the developer workflow and the failure cases they must test.
Designs for fidelity: same API, realistic responses, asynchronous events.
Provides controllable scenarios (declines, disputes, delays, outages).
Makes the move to production safe and simple.
Defines developer-outcome metrics.
outline: Persona: developer integrating payments for the first time; also QA engineers.
Needs: success, declines, 3-D Secure, refunds, disputes, webhooks, delays, outages.
Product: separate test keys; same endpoints; magic test cards and triggers; webhook replay; event log.
Fidelity: identical validation and error formats; differences documented.
Go-live: checklist, key swap, first live payment monitoring.
Metrics: time to first successful test payment; share of integrations that go live without production errors.
questions.reference:
Developers need to test far more than a successful payment: card declines, extra authentication, refunds, disputes, webhooks arriving late or twice, and our own outages. Most production failures come from the paths they could not test.

The product: test-mode keys that hit the same endpoints with the same validation and error formats as production, so code does not change between environments. Special test card numbers and a dashboard let developers trigger scenarios — a decline for insufficient funds, a dispute after seven days, a bank timeout — and replay webhooks. An event log shows exactly what we sent and when. Any behaviour that differs from production is documented.

Going live is a key swap plus a short checklist (webhook signature verification, idempotency keys, error handling), and we watch the first live payments for errors.

Success: time from sign-up to first successful test payment, and — more important — the share of integrations that go live without payment errors in their first week.
pitfalls: A sandbox that only returns success.
Different behaviour from production without documentation.

questions.title: Integration takes days
questions.prompt: Developers say integrating your SMS-sending API takes days instead of hours. Find out why and decide what to fix.
hints: Where exactly do developers get stuck — and how would you find out?
Is the problem the API, the documentation, account setup or regulation?
Which fix helps the most developers soonest?
followups: Most of the delay is waiting for sender registration required by carriers. What can the product do?
Should you build SDKs in more languages?
How do you know the fix worked?
criteria: Measures the funnel from sign-up to first message.
Combines data with direct observation of developers.
Separates product problems from regulatory or account steps.
Prioritises fixes by impact on time to first success.
Measures the result.
outline: Instrument: sign-up → keys → first API call → first delivered message → production volume.
Observe: watch five developers integrate; read support tickets.
Likely causes: account verification, sender registration, confusing errors, missing examples.
Fixes: guided setup; clear error messages with links; quick-start per language; parallelise registration.
Measure time to first delivered message.
questions.reference:
I would measure the integration funnel — sign-up, first API key, first API call, first delivered message, first production traffic — and watch a handful of developers integrate while thinking aloud. Support tickets show where people get stuck.

Often the slow part is not the API at all: carrier rules require sender registration and verification that take days. The product cannot remove the regulation, but it can start registration at sign-up, show its status clearly, and let developers build and test with a shared test sender in the meantime.

Other common fixes: error messages that say what went wrong and how to fix it, a quick-start that works with one copy-paste per language, and a dashboard that shows why a message was not delivered. I would prioritise by how much time each removes for the most developers, and judge success by median time to first delivered message and the share who reach production volume.

questions.title: A public booking API
questions.prompt: Design the public API that lets other companies' software create, change and cancel appointments on your booking platform. Cover the main resources, errors, idempotency, notifications and versioning.
hints: What happens if a client sends the same 'create booking' twice because of a network error?
How do clients learn that a booking changed on your side?
How will you change the API in two years without breaking clients?
followups: Two clients try to book the last slot at the same moment. What happens?
A large partner wants a field only they need. Do you add it?
What limits and quotas would you set?
criteria: Models resources around the user's concepts (availability, booking, customer), not internal tables.
Consistent errors, pagination and naming.
Idempotency keys for creates and payments.
Webhooks with signatures and retries; clients can also poll.
Versioning and deprecation policy from day one; rate limits.
outline: Resources: services, availability (read), bookings (create, read, update, cancel), customers.
Concurrency: holds with expiry or conditional create; clear conflict error.
Idempotency: client-supplied key on POST; same response on retry.
Events: webhooks for booking created/changed/cancelled; signed; retried with backoff; event log endpoint.
Errors: consistent shape with machine code and human message.
Versioning: dated versions; additive changes only within a version; deprecation notice period.
Limits: per-key rate limits with headers; quotas by plan.
questions.reference:
Resources follow the customer’s language: services, availability, bookings and customers. Availability is read-only; bookings support create, read, update and cancel.

Two hard cases. Double submission: every create accepts an idempotency key from the client, and a retry with the same key returns the original result instead of creating a second booking. Concurrency: two clients booking the last slot — one succeeds and the other receives a clear ‘slot no longer available’ error; optionally clients can place a short hold while the end user confirms.

Clients learn about changes through signed webhooks (booking created, changed, cancelled), retried with backoff, plus an events endpoint they can poll if they miss one. Errors share one format: a stable machine-readable code, a human message and a link to documentation.

Versioning starts on day one: within a version we only add fields; breaking changes go in a new dated version with a published deprecation period. Rate limits per key, with headers that tell clients how close they are. A field only one partner needs goes in a general extension mechanism, not the core model.

questions.title: Specifying rate limits
questions.prompt: Abuse on your public API is causing outages. Write the outline of the product spec for introducing rate limits: problem, goals, non-goals, requirements, success metrics and open questions.
hints: Who could be hurt by rate limits you set badly?
What must the spec decide, and what should engineering decide?
How will customers find out they are being limited?
followups: Your largest customer will exceed the default limit on day one. What does the spec say?
Engineering proposes a design in the spec review. How do you respond?
How do you roll this out without breaking customers?
criteria: States the problem with evidence.
Separates goals and explicit non-goals.
Writes requirements as behaviours (what customers experience), not implementation.
Defines success metrics and launch criteria.
Lists open questions with owners; plans rollout and communication.
outline: Problem: abusive and accidental traffic spikes cause outages (evidence: incidents).
Goals: protect availability; predictable limits for good customers.
Non-goals: monetising limits now; per-endpoint pricing.
Requirements: limits per key and per account; clear error with retry-after; headers showing usage; higher limits by request; dashboard visibility.
Rollout: observe-only mode, notify heavy users, gradual enforcement.
Metrics: outages caused by traffic spikes; legitimate requests rejected; support tickets.
Open questions: default values, burst allowance, enterprise exceptions — with owners.
questions.reference:
Problem: three outages last quarter came from single customers sending traffic spikes — some abusive, some accidental retry loops. Goal: protect availability for everyone with limits that good customers rarely notice. Non-goals: charging for higher limits now; per-endpoint pricing.

Requirements are written as customer-visible behaviour: each API key has a limit and short bursts are allowed; a request over the limit gets a clear error and a ‘retry after’ time; every response shows remaining capacity; customers can see their usage in the dashboard and request higher limits. How the limiter works is left to engineering.

Rollout: first run in observe-only mode to see who would be limited; contact those customers; then enforce gradually. Success: zero outages from traffic spikes, a very small share of legitimate requests rejected, and no rise in support tickets.

Open questions with owners: default numbers (engineering + data), handling of the largest customers (account management), and whether limits differ by plan (product). When engineering proposes a design in review, that is welcome — the spec defines behaviour; the design is theirs.
pitfalls: No rollout plan for existing heavy users.

questions.title: Search: build or buy?
questions.prompt: Your developer platform needs full-text search across customers' data. Engineering wants to build it on an open-source engine; a vendor offers a managed search service. How do you decide?
hints: Is search core to why customers choose you?
What does each option cost over three years, including people?
What happens to customers' data with a vendor?
followups: The vendor's price doubles in year two. How would you have protected against that?
Engineering is excited to build. How do you handle the conversation if you choose to buy?
What would make you revisit the decision?
criteria: Asks whether search is a differentiator.
Compares total cost of ownership including operations.
Assesses time to market and opportunity cost.
Considers data security, residency and lock-in.
Decides with a review trigger and an exit plan.
outline: Strategic: is search a reason customers pick us, or hygiene?
TCO over three years: licence/usage vs engineers to build and operate, on-call, scaling.
Time to market: vendor faster; build gives control.
Risk: data handling, residency, outage dependency, pricing changes, lock-in.
Decision + abstraction layer + exit plan + review triggers.
questions.reference:
I would first ask whether search is a reason customers choose us. If it is hygiene — they expect it but choose us for other reasons — the bar for building is high.

Then compare total cost over three years. The vendor: usage fees growing with data volume, plus integration work. Building: engineers to build and run the cluster, on-call, scaling work, and what those engineers would otherwise build. Then time to market and risk: where the vendor stores customer data, whether it meets our residency commitments, what happens when it has an outage, and how hard it is to leave.

If search is not a differentiator and the vendor meets our data commitments, I would buy, behind an internal interface so we can switch later, with contract terms that cap price increases. If search quality is central to our product, building on an open-source engine makes sense. In either case I would set triggers to revisit — cost per customer above a threshold, or a requirement the vendor cannot meet — and explain the reasoning to engineering openly.

questions.title: Is the new SDK working?
questions.prompt: You shipped a new mobile SDK for your analytics product three months ago. How do you know whether it is succeeding?
hints: What does a developer try to achieve with the SDK?
Downloads are not adoption. What is?
How would you spot integrations that started and failed?
followups: Downloads are high, active integrations low. Diagnose.
Which metric would you put in front of the VP?
How do you get qualitative signals from developers?
criteria: Defines activation as successful data flowing in production.
Tracks time to first event and integration retention.
Measures reliability (crash rate, app size, performance impact).
Includes support and documentation signals.
Connects to business outcome (accounts expanding usage).
outline: Goal: developers send correct events from production apps.
Activation: first production event from a new app; time to reach it.
Retention: apps still sending events after 30/90 days; versions in use.
Quality: crash rate attributed to SDK; app size; battery and network impact; error events.
Support: tickets per integration; doc search failures.
Business: accounts using SDK data in dashboards; expansion.
questions.reference:
The SDK succeeds if developers get correct data flowing from real apps and keep it flowing. So the primary metric is the number of production apps actively sending events, with time from first download to first production event as the key input.

I would track the funnel — download, first test event, first production event, still active after 90 days — to see where integrations die. Quality matters as much: crashes attributed to the SDK, its effect on app size and battery, and malformed events. A crash in someone else’s app destroys trust quickly.

Support tickets per new integration and documentation searches that end without a click show friction. And the business view: are accounts that use the SDK actually using the data — dashboards viewed, more seats bought?

If downloads are high but production apps are low, I would look at the step between test and production: often configuration or privacy-consent setup is unclear.
pitfalls: Ignoring the SDK's impact on host apps.

questions.title: Retiring version 1
questions.prompt: Your API's version 1 is used by 3,000 customers and blocks important improvements. Plan its deprecation.
hints: Why would customers move? What is in it for them?
Who are the hardest customers to move?
What happens on the shutdown date to customers who have not moved?
followups: A top-ten customer says they cannot migrate this year. What do you do?
How do you track progress?
What would you never do during a deprecation?
criteria: Makes version 2 clearly better and migration easy (guides, tools, compatibility).
Segments customers by usage and effort.
Sets a timeline with notice periods and milestones.
Provides direct help for the hardest cases; handles exceptions deliberately.
Communicates repeatedly; enforces the end date with safeguards (brownouts).
outline: Value: features and performance only in v2; migration guide and automated tooling.
Segment: by traffic and endpoints used; identify the long tail and the hardest.
Timeline: announcement; no new v1 sign-ups; reminders; scheduled brownouts; shutdown.
Help: office hours; engineering help for top customers; paid exceptions with end dates.
Track: share of traffic and customers on v2.
Communicate in the dashboard, email, API response headers.
questions.reference:
Customers move when the new version is better and moving is easy. So v2 must offer things v1 cannot, with a migration guide, side-by-side examples and, where possible, a tool that rewrites calls.

I would segment the 3,000 customers by traffic and the v1 features they use: most will be simple; a few heavy users will be hard. The timeline: announce with a long notice period; stop new v1 sign-ups; send reminders through email, the dashboard and API response headers; then run short scheduled ‘brownouts’ where v1 is briefly unavailable, so forgotten integrations reveal themselves before the final date.

Top customers get direct engineering help. If one genuinely cannot move this year, I would agree a time-limited exception in writing, possibly with a support fee, rather than delay the shutdown for everyone. Progress is tracked weekly by share of customers and traffic on v2. What I would never do: shut down without warning or move the date repeatedly — both teach customers to ignore deprecations.
pitfalls: No brownouts or warnings in responses.

questions.title: The what, not the how
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you disagreed with engineers about a technical product decision. How did you separate what the product needed from how it should be built?
hints: What was the product requirement, and what was the engineering choice?
Did you hold the requirement or the solution?
What did you learn about working with engineers?
followups: Did you ever overrule an engineering decision?
How technical do you think a technical PM should be?
What would the engineers say about you?
criteria: Distinguishes requirement from implementation.
Uses technical understanding to ask good questions, not to dictate.
Holds the line on user needs.
Resolution respected engineering ownership.
Specific outcome and lesson.
outline: Situation and decision.
The requirement you cared about.
The engineering approach and your concern.
How you resolved it (criteria, prototype, data).
Outcome.
Lesson.
questions.reference: A strong answer (a model of structure, not a script): “Engineering wanted webhooks delivered in batches every minute to save infrastructure cost. My concern was the requirement: our customers needed to react to failed payments within seconds. I wrote down the requirement — 95% of events delivered within five seconds — rather than arguing for a design. The team found a way to stream events and still batch internally, meeting the target at modest extra cost. I learned to argue for the requirement with numbers and leave the design to the people who build it.”
pitfalls: Giving in on a real user need.
